#9838. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

#9837. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9836. Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The new YubiID service bridges identity verification with credential enrollment and recovery across existing identity platforms, closing a phishing-resistant authentication gap. Plus: post-quantum YubiKey beta.

Yubico wants to help employers verify a person’s identity before enrolling login credentials — and again when the employee needs to regain access after losing a key or mobile device.

On Tuesday, the maker of YubiKey authentication devices unveiled YubiID, a subscription service entering limited early access that links identity verification with credential enrollment and account recovery. Announced at Yubico's inaugural YubiNation user conference in San Francisco this week, the service integrates with major identity providers, including Microsoft Entra, Okta, and Ping, and supports enrolling credentials on YubiKeys and mobile phones. This extends Yubico's reach to organizations that have decided against deploying hardware keys.

The launch addresses a growing recognition that protecting a login to be phishing-resistant is no longer enough. It does not establish that the right person received the credential, or that someone requesting a replacement is the legitimate owner. Yubico field CTO Derek Hanson described that shift at the FIDO Alliance's Authenticate conference last month, saying the help desk "has moved from an operational control to an actual security control in most enterprises."

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

Yubico is working with a group of unnamed "large organizations" as design partners and hopes to make YubiID generally available in the first half of 2027, CEO Jerrod Chong tells Dark Reading. The company has not revealed pricing.

According to Chong, the problem YubiID addresses used to be an afterthought: confirming that a key reaches the right person and that someone reporting it as lost is indeed that person. The new service provides a baseline identity-verification capability, but customers can also use their own verification process or rely on other providers. Planned integrations with Clear, Nametag, and HYPR will allow organizations to combine providers whose coverage differs by region.

For most enterprises, this is a familiar scenario: employees prove their identities to HR in one part of the office, then collect their login credentials from IT in another part of the office. Connecting these steps reduces opportunities for impersonation because identity verification is required for both initial enrollment and enrollment of replacement credentials.

"Recovery is such a weak spot for credential management," Andrew Shikiar, executive director and CEO of the FIDO Alliance, tells Dark Reading. Digital identity credentials provide enterprises with a way to reestablish a user's identity during recovery without relying on knowledge-based secrets, Shikiar says. Solving the recovery challenge involves more than just technology; it also requires policy, regulatory alignment, user behavior change, and business process design.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

For organizations already investing in Okta, Ping, or Microsoft Entra, YubiID coordinates verification and enrollment; it does not replace those identity platforms. Yubico has built connectors to enroll credentials from those providers and also supports homegrown identity systems.

"We're not being an IDP," Chong says. "I think that there are more opportunities for collaboration than competition."

The practical benefit is tighter coordination. An organization can connect its chosen verification process to enrollment in the identity systems employees already use, rather than managing those steps as disconnected workflows. That becomes especially relevant for enterprises running multiple identity providers, where the employee's immediate need is simply to receive working credentials, regardless of which platform manages the account.

For a company onboarding 10,000 temporary workers ahead of the holiday season, YubiID can support both administrator-assisted, in-person enrollment and remote enrollment and verification, giving the company multiple ways to connect identity checks to access setup. The benefit, Chong says, is as much operational as security-related — fewer disconnected steps between verifying a worker and getting that person authenticated — though he did not provide figures on potential time savings or reductions in help-desk work. Interest is strongest among organizations with large, distributed or seasonal workforces, including transportation, retail, healthcare, consulting, and global services companies.

Related:Flaws in Passkey Implementation Show Old Attacks Still Work

Yubico is entering a market where identity providers and verification specialists already offer overlapping onboarding and recovery capabilities. Microsoft Entra's verified account recovery became generally available in May, using identity verification to help users regain access and register authentication methods without relying on a conventional manual help-desk process. Nametag and HYPR—both planned YubiID integration partners—also sell workforce verification and recovery capabilities. Beyond Identity already connects Nametag's identity checks to passkey enrollment and recovery, while 1Kosmos combines identity verification with passwordless authentication.

Chong maintains YubiID's differentiator is connecting verification and enrollment across platforms, rather than tying the workflow to a single identity provider. Yubico also brings its hardware business into those relationships: it makes the devices where many customers' authentication credentials reside. Chong connects that experience with the challenge of distributing keys, verifying recipients, and enrolling replacements across a global workforce.

Hardware is not required. Support for credentials on mobile devices could appeal to customers who find hardware key distribution too difficult. Those customers haven't necessarily rejected the keys' security benefits; rather, the logistics are "sometimes quite challenging," Chong says.

Federal agencies could also use employees' existing PIV credentials to establish their identities when enrolling FIDO credentials on YubiKeys or mobile authenticators, Chong says, while noting that those workflows are future potential capabilities and not fully available at launch.

Separately, Yubico announced a public beta program for a post-quantum-ready YubiKey. The beta YubiKey will support NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms, but Yubico did not specify which ones. Yubico has tested early implementations with Chrome and Firefox, with early keys sent to federal labs and hyperscalers. Yubico expects to submit the key for FIPS validation within about a year, depending on beta testing and customer feedback, although completion is not guaranteed.

Despite being "crypto-agile," Chong confirms the beta devices cannot receive firmware upgrades, meaning organizations would later need to replace those keys if different algorithms are required. "Doing firmware upgrades safely across the web is not trivial," he says.

A June executive order directs agencies to transition high-value assets and high-impact systems to post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031. Organizations evaluating the beta keys will need to test both the new cryptography and the process for replacing and enrolling devices.

Yubico ultimately envisions providing verifiable proof that a person authorized a specific AI agent action, but Chong confirms that agent-authorization capabilities are not part of this launch. While the combination of Yubico's backend services, applications, and hardware keys forms the foundation for additional use cases, for now the YubiID service focuses on verifying people, enrolling credentials, and handling recovery.

"In a simple way to look at it, we're offering an end-to-end solution rather than just a YubiKey solution," Chong says.

#9835. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9834. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9833. Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

An unknown operator appears to have exfiltrated SQL Server backups from the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration in under a half hour.

An unknown threat actor managed to gain access to sensitive databases belonging to the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration, exfiltrating nearly 69GB of information on workers, contracts, and financial records, according to an analysis of a staging server used in the breach.

Over 24 minutes, the attacker copied 27 backup databases with information on overseas-employment case management, including accreditation, contracts, and cashier and LandBank records, according to threat intelligence firm Hunt.io's Oct. 28 analysis of the logs found on a Singaporean staging server used by the attacker. The cyberattackers used privileged escalation tools, namely GodPotato and SeImpersonate, and the Impacket network library for Python to move the data, but the trail stopped at the staging server, says Esteban Borges, head of research for Hunt.io.

The server had been later accessed, but by who is not clear, Borges says. While Hunt.io has not yet discovered the data as advertised for sale, the information may have been detected and removed, but that seems unlikely, he says.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

"I won't claim the backups stopped on the staging server," he says, so it's "still a breach, since the data was copied out of the agency’s control and the log shows the transfer completing."

This is not the first time that cybersecurity firms have found evidence that Philippine government data had been stolen. In August, Hunt.io discovered another threat actor's workspace hosting a number of tools and, in that case, 1.2GB of data stolen from a Philippine nuclear regulatory agency and a maritime shipbuilding contractor. A year ago, Philippine police arrested the mayor of a small town after discovering she was a Chinese national posing as a Filipina citizen and operating a cyber-scam center.

Whether the current incident involved China or cybercriminal groups is not clear. While Hunt.io did find some Chinese language fragments in the parts of the code, that code belonged to a third-party software library; thus, Hunt.io did not attribute the hack. The company did say, however, that both cybercriminals and nation-state adversaries would find value in the personally identifiable information (PII).

"That kind of migrant-worker PII, plus contract and payment data, is useful for fraud and identity theft, so it has commercial value," Borges says. "It's also a detailed map of a diaspora population, which can interest a state actor."

The latest insight into attacks on the Philippine government came after Hunt.io researchers discovered an open directory on a server hosted on the Singaporean address space of a Helsinki-based firm UpCloud Ltd., the analysis stated. The open directory contained tools and logs files for the attack, including a rebranded version of the GodPotato privilege escalation library, a PowerShell stager to unpack tools in memory, and the full Impacket Python environment.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

While Hunt.io considered the incident a confirmed compromise, the lack of runtime telemetry meant that Borges could not answer where the attacker moved the data.

"[W]e still can’t answer ... how they got in, whether the payload ran, and where the data went," he says.

However, the tools and the attacker's process indicated an operator with some strong ability, but who also made some simple mistakes, Borges says.

"The payload engineering is competent, [but] the operational security is poor — they left the staging server and its logs wide open," he says. "[It was] someone who can build the tool properly but was careless about keeping their own server quiet. I wouldn't call that top-tier or amateur."

The impact of the breach may boil down to the identity of the attacker and what they do with the stolen data. While Hunt.io notified the CERT Philippines (CERT-PH) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), the company declined to provide any more details of the national responses to the leak.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

However, Borges did say that, so far, the information has not appeared for sale on the Dark Web.

"We haven't seen the backups surface for sale or in a leak," he says. "We never opened the backups themselves."

Governments in the region need to scan their own networks and lock down their attack surface area, he says. Workers with too many privileges allow attackers with tools such as SeImpersonate to gain more access to assets on the network. Hunt.io also found that the migrant-worker portal exposed a number of risky ports, including SMB on 445 and WinRM on 5985 and 47001.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9832. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9831. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9830. Self-host live updates for Capacitor with Codemagic Patch

Codemagic Patch ships live updates of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to Capacitor, Ionic, and Cordova-on-Capacitor apps, without a new store binary.

Say a checkout button stops working on some Android 15 devices, and the fix turns out to be four lines of TypeScript. In a Capacitor app, those four lines live in the web layer, inside a WebView, nowhere near native code. Without over-the-air (OTA) updates, they still have to go the long way round: new binary, store submission, review, and then a slow trickle of users who eventually update. Some never do.

That’s the problem OTA updates solve. While we originally developed it for React Native apps, Codemagic Patch now also supports Capacitor apps with our self-hosted tool.

Patch v0.6.0 ships with two new packages: @codemagic/capacitor-patch, the SDK that goes into your app, and @codemagic/capacitor-patch-cli, a command line made for publishing and managing Capacitor releases. They use the same server, dashboard, and delivery protocol as our React Native SDK.

Below, we’ll go through what you get with Patch, why Capacitor turned out to be the simplest framework we’ve ever built OTA support for, how you can self-host Patch, and where to find the docs to get your first release out.

Ionic has announced that all Appflow features and services will be sunset on December 31, 2027, a little over a year from now. They’ll keep Appflow up to date with its dependencies until then. After that, Ionic warns that apps still depending on Appflow may hit failed builds and failed live updates, and users may end up looking at a blank white screen.

A year can feel like plenty of time. It isn’t, once you account for how an OTA migration works. Your new SDK has to ship inside a native binary. That binary has to pass review and then actually get installed by enough of your users, because every device still on the old SDK will keep asking the old service for updates. In practice, the migration build should be out months before the deadline.

We’ve been building, signing, and publishing Capacitor apps on Codemagic for years, and Ionic’s own continuity page lists us as an alternative for Appflow native builds. Capacitor teams could also already get OTA updates from our CodePush service through the community cap-codepush plugin. Patch replaces that arrangement with a first-party SDK that we design, test, and support ourselves. For a Capacitor team, that means native builds and live updates from one vendor.

A server you can run yourself, an SDK in the app, a CLI to publish the web build you already produce, and a dashboard for what happened after that.

The Codemagic Patch dashboard with example data

OTA for React Native is a fairly involved piece of engineering. The tooling has to deal with a bundler (Metro or Expo), Hermes bytecode, and the New Architecture, and it has to hook into both how the bundle is built and how the runtime loads it.

Capacitor has none of that. A Capacitor app is a native shell that points a WebView at a folder of web assets, and @capacitor/core already has the APIs to change which folder that is (setServerBasePath, getServerBasePath, and persistServerBasePath). An OTA update comes down to downloading a new folder, verifying it, and pointing Capacitor at it on the next launch. There’s no bundler to integrate with and no bytecode format to match.

You see the same thing in the CLI. cmpatch-capacitor doesn’t run your build and doesn’t care whether you’ve run npx cap sync. You build the way you already do (ionic build, ng build, vite build), and whatever lands in your webDir is the release. It doesn’t matter whether that’s Angular, React, Vue, or Svelte.

Fewer moving parts means fewer ways for an update to break your app, and for an update mechanism that’s the property that counts most.

There’s one rule every team should understand before shipping their first Capacitor OTA release, because it’s much cheaper to learn it now than in production.

Your web bundle calls into native code: Capacitor plugins, your own native classes, native configuration. A bundle built for one native build can break on another. If your new web code calls Camera.getPhoto() and the installed binary shipped before you added @capacitor/camera, it will fail.

The Capacitor CLI doesn’t try to detect this by fingerprinting your native project. Every release instead targets one exact native app version (CFBundleShortVersionString on iOS, versionName on Android) and is only delivered to that version. Ranges and wildcards aren’t accepted. In day-to-day terms:

If your team already versions carefully, you’ll hardly notice this. If it doesn’t, OTA will push you into the habit, and you’ll be better off for it. The binary version filter added to the Patch dashboard’s deployment and Metrics pages in this release makes it easy to see how each version is doing.

Put together, every change goes down one of two paths:

Build your web assets, publish them with cmpatch-capacitor release create against the current binary version, test on Staging, then promote to Production with a staged rollout.

Bump the native version, then build, sign, and publish through Codemagic. Once the new binary is through review and in users’ hands, future OTA releases target the new version.

OTA is easy to oversell, so it’s worth being specific.

The obvious win is speed. A web-layer fix stops taking days of review and update lag and starts reaching users within minutes of publishing, as soon as their devices check in. For a consumer app, that can be the difference between a wave of one-star reviews and nobody noticing. For a B2B or internal app, it’s the difference between an escalation and a ticket closed the same afternoon.

You also end up supporting fewer versions. With store-only updates, every version a user hasn’t bothered to update is still out there, still generating bug reports. With OTA, devices on the same binary converge on the same web bundle, so “can’t reproduce” happens a lot less.

And your two release cycles can run at their own pace. The native release train can stay as deliberate as your compliance process requires, monthly or quarterly, while the web layer ships whenever your team is ready. Staging, staged rollouts, and promotion give you a controlled route from merge to full rollout.

What OTA can’t do is ship native code, and the app stores are explicit about where that line is.

Apple’s Developer Program License Agreement, section 3.3.1(B) forbids apps from downloading executable code but allows interpreted code, which is what the JavaScript in a Capacitor WebView is. There are conditions. The downloaded code can’t change the app’s primary purpose by adding features that don’t match how the app was described and advertised. It can’t get around signing, sandboxing, or other OS security features. And it can’t turn the app into a store for other apps.

Google Play’s Device and Network Abuse policy starts from a stricter position. Apps may not update themselves outside Google Play or download executable code such as dex, JAR, or .so files from anywhere else. The policy then makes an exception for code that runs in an interpreter or virtual machine with only indirect access to Android APIs, and gives “JavaScript in a webview or browser” as its example. That code still can’t be used to break any other Play policy.

So both stores end up in the same place. Bug fixes, copy changes, UI tweaks, and incremental improvements to the app people already installed are fine. Using OTA to turn the app into something other than what was reviewed is not, and it puts your developer account at risk. Signed releases help with the security side of Apple’s conditions, and keeping your native versions disciplined keeps native changes inside reviewed binaries, where they belong.

A lot of OTA services only come as a hosted product. Patch can be either.

The server, release worker, and dashboard run on your infrastructure as a single Docker Compose deployment: Caddy for TLS, the Patch server, PostgreSQL, and S3-compatible object storage, with Cloudflare or CloudFront in front if you want a CDN. Your bundles, metrics, and release history stay on your network. The Capacitor SDK talks to the standard Patch server without any changes, so you set up the server once with the self-hosting guide, and cmpatch-capacitor handles everything Capacitor-specific from there.

The SDKs and CLIs are licensed under Apache 2.0. The server uses the Codemagic Server License, which is free for up to 1,000,000 monthly active devices and converts to Apache 2.0 two years after each release. The only thing you can’t do is resell Patch as a competing OTA service.

To try it before provisioning anything, run the local evaluation stack. It runs the real server, database, storage, and dashboard on your machine in Docker, and the Capacitor CLI can point straight at it:

The local server has a prefilled one-click login, so there’s no account to create.

Self-hosting makes the most sense for teams with strict data residency rules, regulated or air-gapped environments, or a preference for owning their infrastructure.

A free license doesn’t make infrastructure free. Somebody has to keep the server patched, look after the database, manage TLS and the CDN, and be on call when a release goes wrong. Plenty of teams would rather put that time into their app.

Hosted Patch runs the same software on our infrastructure. The first 100,000 monthly active users are free, there are no limits on updates or bandwidth, and the rest of the pricing is on our pricing page. Larger teams can get enterprise plans, dedicated servers, and geolocated servers that keep update infrastructure and data in a specific region.

Email sales@codemagic.io to talk about it.

The Patch documentation covers setup step by step, so this is an overview of the path from nothing to your first OTA release.

1. Decide where Patch runs. Self-host with the self-hosting guide, or talk to our team about hosted service. For a first look, the local stack above is enough.

2. Install the CLI and create one Patch app per platform. Each app comes with Staging and Production deployments, each with its own deployment key. Don’t let iOS and Android share a deployment. A release’s delivery path doesn’t include the platform, so the two would overwrite each other.

3. Add the SDK to your Capacitor project. It supports the two most recent Capacitor major versions (currently 7 and 8) and Android minSdkVersion 24 or higher.

Configuration goes in capacitor.config.ts, with one block per platform. The API URL and download base URL come from your Patch server: the self-host installer prints both, and we give them to you for hosted Patch.

Then call start() once the app has rendered its first screen:

Where you call it matters. start() is what tells the SDK the running bundle is healthy, so call it after your UI is actually up, not early in bootstrap. That way an update that crashes during startup still gets rolled back. Two more tips: every config value can also be set as a native resource (Info.plist or strings.xml) if you inject per-environment values in CI, and npx codemagic-patch-check-config is worth adding to your native build workflow to catch a shared deployment key before it ships. The check reads JSON only, so if your config is capacitor.config.ts, run it after npx cap sync and point it at the synced copy: npx codemagic-patch-check-config android/app/src/main/assets/capacitor.config.json. The Patch docs cover native setup for Capacitor, checking for updates, install modes, and the step-by-step APIs, and the SDK reference lists everything the SDK exports. Pick Capacitor in the switcher at the top of the docs menu to see the Capacitor version of each page.

4. Publish a release to Staging from the CLI. Build the web assets the way you already do, then publish that folder once per platform. --target-binary-version has to be the native version you will ship in the next step (CFBundleShortVersionString on iOS, versionName on Android). www below is the webDir from capacitor.config.ts.

Each command publishes one platform. Install a build that includes the SDK and uses that same native version if you want to try the Staging release on a device before it goes to the stores.

5. Ship the native release, then publish Production from CI. The SDK has to be in the installed app before a device can receive an update, so this first binary is a normal store release. Build, sign, and publish it through Codemagic as usual. CI/CD for Ionic apps walks through connecting the repo and a first workflow, and the Ionic Capacitor build guide covers code signing, versioning, and publishing for both platforms.

After that, Production releases belong in CI. Create a token with cmpatch-capacitor token create, store it with your server URL and the deployment IDs from deployment list, and publish from the pipeline. The first release guide covers that workflow, including promotion and staged rollouts.

Most Appflow concepts carry over directly. Appflow channels become Patch deployments, and you get Staging and Production from the start. A few things work differently, and it’s better to know about them before you start:

None of these should stop you, but the first one decides your timeline. The Appflow migration guide walks through the swap.

If you’re already using our CodePush service with cap-codepush, nothing changes for you today. When you’re ready, the move to Patch follows the same pattern: one native release with the new SDK, then you publish with cmpatch-capacitor instead of code-push.

We’d rather you choose the right tool than the wrong one from us, so here are the cases where Patch won’t help much.

Most of your changes are native. Plugin upgrades, Capacitor version bumps, and native features all need a reviewed binary whichever OTA service you use. For teams like that, a fast and reliable native build-and-publish setup matters more, and Codemagic handles that too.

Your beta program depends on runtime channel switching. The Patch Capacitor SDK doesn’t offer it today. Separate beta builds work, but it’s a different workflow, so think it through before migrating.

Your native versioning is a mess and you can’t fix it. Exact-version targeting will feel strict. We think strict is the safer default, because it makes the compatibility boundary visible instead of guessing at it, but it does ask for some discipline.

You’re happy on Appflow right now. You don’t have to move tomorrow. You do have to move before the end of 2027, and the native release the swap requires means you should start well before that.

No. Capacitor does not ship an updater. Codemagic Patch is a separate SDK, @codemagic/capacitor-patch, and a CLI, cmpatch-capacitor.

It can replace Appflow Live Updates for web-layer releases. Appflow shuts down on December 31, 2027, and the Patch SDK has to ship inside a native binary well before that, because devices still on the old SDK keep calling Appflow.

You can self-host the server for free for up to 1,000,000 monthly active devices. Hosted Patch is for companies above that, and you arrange it with us. There is no signup.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in the web layer can go out over the air, targeted at one exact native version. Plugin changes, native code, and native config still need a store release with a bumped version.

Capacitor is the simplest framework we’ve built OTA support for, and it now has its own Patch SDK and CLI, with binary diffs, automatic crash-loop rollback, signed releases, and staged rollouts with promotion, plus checks for the mistakes that most often turn into blank screens. You can run Patch yourself, free for up to a 1M monthly active users (MAU), or have us host it, with a free tier available for under 100k MAU. Enterprise plans offer dedicated or geolocated servers, and engineers who’ll work through your compliance requirements with you. Together with the Capacitor build, signing, and publishing support Codemagic already has, that covers the whole release process on one platform.

This is the first release of the Capacitor SDK and CLI (v0.1.0). The Patch release notes have the full changelog, and we’d love to hear how it works for you.

If Appflow’s shutdown is on your roadmap, start before it becomes urgent. Spin up the local evaluation stack this week, and put the SDK in your next native release.
