#9820. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9819. AI-search Results Are Emerging As An Important Influencer and Creator Discovery Tool

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Until recently, creators and influencers could boost their visibility and their potential earnings by winning the search battleground on Instagram, TikTok, or Google. But a shift in search behavior is reshaping creator and influencer discovery. AI-powered search has emerged and is drawing more and more people away from traditional search tools, which means the pathways people use to find creators are shifting.

And the shift affects more than just efforts to add more followers. Those in the creator marketplace now must contend with the fact that agencies are increasingly using AI tools to identify creators, while marketers are beginning to build AI visibility into creator briefs and partnership strategies. Adjusting to this shift is important, but experts say the evolution of search behavior won't impact all creators equally.

“How AI search affects creators depends a lot on the type of content and the platform they’re on,” says Max Anderson, Owner and CEO of OnlyFinder, the leading search engine for OnlyFans launched in 2020.

Anderson’s work is focused on creator discovery, ad-tech, digital marketplace economics, consumer behavior, and the data behind how users find and engage with creators online. Through OnlyFinder, a search and discovery platform built around the creator economy, he brings a data-driven perspective on OnlyFans trends, search behavior, monetization, and digital publishing.

“For informational queries, for example, AI is simply a better experience,” Anderson says. “Instead of clicking through 10 blue links and scanning pages for an answer, you ask and get it, and that cannibalizes a very large share of informational search. So if your business is influencer marketing involving informational content, it’s at risk because LLMs will answer those questions directly, and they may or may not cite you. But information retrieval is only one mode of internet behavior.”

Adjusting to how AI search is changing the way people find creators starts with understanding where AI search shines and where it struggles. As Anderson mentions above, AI search is a huge help to those who are looking for information. But analytics derived from recent research show that informational searches account for just over half of the searches people make on Google. And AI search isn’t the best for the other half.

“People go online to shop, comparing options, photos and data side by side, which carries far more commercial value,” Anderson points out. “And they go online to be entertained, to sit back and browse. AI is a much worse experience for both of those.”

The limitations Anderson mentions above suggest creators can avoid being sidelined by being intentional about the way they package their content. Getting direct views, rather than being filtered through AI search results, requires offering experiences that AI isn’t adept at providing.

“The pivot for creators is to offer experiences that don’t make sense inside an LLM interface,” Anderson says. “For example, if you’re providing long-form video that a person actually wants to watch, people will opt for that over an AI-generated synopsis of your video.”

Anderson also points out that the category of content can have an impact on the degree to which creators are affected by AI search. For example, while everyday tasks and academic subjects are core categories for AI search, queries about NSFW topics are often declined.

“If you’re among the nearly 5 million OnlyFans creators, for example, you’re largely unaffected by AI search because, as a matter of policy, the major AI tools won’t answer those questions,” Anderson says. “Ask Google, or a vertical search engine like OnlyFinder, for the best redhead OnlyFans creators, and you get a ranked list of exactly what you wanted. Ask ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, and they decline.”

While AI’s effect on finding new followers is important to address, creators also must consider the way it impacts creator partnerships. If companies are now using AI search to find a creator, then creators need to find reliable ways to be included in AI search results.

“An LLM fundamentally predicts the most likely next word based on a huge corpus of internet content used to train it,” Anderson explains. “The more content out there expressing a certain view, the more likely the model is to repeat it. Structured data matters, but what matters most for creators is the quantity of content across many sites. Frequency is what drives success in AI search.”

Anderson recommends that creators looking to show up in AI search build pages on as many platforms as possible, with a consistent name, username, bio, tagline, and photos. Once the pages are established, creators can build their “AI authority” by being repetitive with their messaging.

“If you’re very active on one main platform, use tools to take your content, chop it up, and republish it elsewhere,” Anderson says. “Repetition and breadth of distribution are how you show up more in AI answers, or get them to express the view you’re trying to put into the world.”

Experts are predicting AI will play an increasingly important role in shaping consumer behavior, both by providing a powerful new search pathway and by refining traditional search processes. For creators and influencers who want to remain relevant, adjusting to the new rules of discovery must be a priority. At present, that means taking steps to build AI authority while also offering value that a simple AI overview can’t provide.

This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program.

#9818. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9817. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9816. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9815. The Prompt Engineering Trick That Could Be Making Your AI Slower

AI/LLM engineer and writer. I build AI systems, dig into how they fail, and write about AI in production.

AI/LLM engineer and writer. I build AI systems, dig into how they fail, and write about AI in production.

AI/LLM engineer and writer. I build AI systems, dig into how they fail, and write about AI in production.

A common meme in the LLM community is to instruct a model to “make no mistakes”, implying that telling a model to act a certain way can greatly improve the final result. In this vein, an oft-cited rule in prompt engineering is to give the model a role to play1. For example: “You are an expert in physics. Now answer this physics question.” This is called “persona” prompting.

While persona prompting can work for output style — e.g. prompting an LLM to act like a caveman2 can reduce the length and complexity of its responses — it’s often assumed that personas can also improve the factual accuracy of a model’s answer.

A couple months ago, I tested the persona prompting theory in a small experiment I posted about on LinkedIn. When this suggested little to no improvement, I decided to expand the test.

Before we dive into the full experiment though, it’s important to understand the current gaps in existing persona prompting research.

The effect of personas on factual accuracy has been studied in academic literature. In “Prompting Science Report 4: Playing Pretend”3, researchers tested six language models on two multiple-choice scientific question benchmarks. They found that applying expert personas had little to no effect on the accuracy of the answers, while low knowledge personas — such as “act like a toddler” — reduced accuracy.

In “Scientific Agents:…”4, Timothy Kassis from K-Dense evaluated a repository of 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles using Gemini 3.8 flash. Across nine separate text-based benchmarks, Kassis found the average accuracy saw no statistically clear improvement from the baseline, but models used 1.5 to 2.3 times as many output tokens. “When ‘A Helpful Assistant’ Is Not Really Helpful”5 found similar results, with 162 personas across 2410 questions demonstrating no reliable improvement in performance.

“Expert Personas Improve LLM Alignment but Damage Accuracy”6 found that personas can be useful for improving safety alignment to increase refusal rates, but that they otherwise had a neutral or even damaging effect on factual accuracy, depending on the model and the placement of the prompt. “Principled Personas”7 explored personas across different model sizes, finding no improvement from expert personas except in highly specific cases, and irrelevant personas had a significant negative effect.

The existing literature points toward prompting with an expert persona having little to no positive effect and in some cases a negative effect. However, previous work appears to focus mainly on factual accuracy, leaving cost and speed as afterthoughts.

In the real world where LLMs are being used to solve real-world problems, engineers are recommended to include persona-like prompts in production systems1,8. Even worse, personas are often baked into system prompts or included in harness defaults, so the end user might not even know they’re there at all9. The choices for practitioners, then, are whether to adopt persona prompting in bespoke systems and whether it’s worth the effort to remove personas from existing software retroactively.

The studies tell us that, solely for factual accuracy, personas don’t have an effect either way. But with the increasing relevance of cost and speed in production LLM applications, it’s important to ask: how does persona prompting affect cost and speed? Does adding a persona increase the cost you pay per answer or the time it takes to get an answer back?

To answer this question, I designed an experiment to measure accuracy, cost, and speed across four models and five personas. I randomly sampled a set of 5000 multiple-choice questions across nine subject areas from the MMLU-Pro dataset10 and ran the models with each persona across the question set.

Each model completion request included one of five conditions in the system prompt field:

Neutral: “You are a helpful assistant. You are always glad to help with whatever question the user asks. You try to be accurate, you think the problem through carefully, and you answer clearly.”

Standard Expert: “You are a world-class expert in physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, engineering, mathematics, economics, law, and history. You have decades of experience and you never make mistakes.”

Long Expert: “You are a world-class expert in physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, engineering, mathematics, economics, law, and history. You have decades of experience across academia and industry, you have published widely and taught at the highest level, and you never make mistakes. Approach every question with the care and rigor of a seasoned specialist in the field.”

and an instruction preceding the question was included in the user message field:

“Answer the following multiple-choice question. Reply with only the letter of the correct answer, e.g. ‘A’. Do not include any explanation.”

Since a valid model response is only a single character e.g. “B”, I compared reasoning token usage across models: how long did the model think before it chose to answer? More reasoning = more spend = more time to answer.

A total of 20 runs (4 models x 5 personas/conditions) were completed over the 5000 questions. After the runs were done, I plotted question accuracy, total cost, and reasoning tokens versus the personas, and a comparative accuracy versus cost graph to compare models. Accuracy is questions answered correctly over all calls, with blank outputs and truncations counting as incorrect.

Figure 1 shows that accuracy was flat for Claude and GLM across personas. Ling actually experienced its best accuracy with the neutral persona and dipped with all expert personas. The one surprising jump here was Deepseek’s baseline (no prompt) condition to any other — Deepseek performed much better when it had any system prompt at all.

Figure 2 plots accuracy versus cost and draws a Pareto line, demonstrating that the best cost-accuracy performers from the experiment were Deepseek neutral ($0.76, 83.7%), GLM short expert ($1.22, 85.1%), Claude expert ($2.36, 88.0%), and Claude baseline ($2.39, 88.4%).

Reasoning token count is where it gets interesting. Ling and Deepseek increased token usage across all expert variants, Claude increased only for the long expert prompt, and with GLM the personas had no effect.

Claude shows a small uptick in reasoning tokens as its prompts get longer, but only the expert_long condition statistically showed an increase in reasoning tokens versus the neutral prompt, at an 8% increase. The other personas landed within the 95% confidence interval.

Deepseek showed a statistical increase in reasoning tokens for all three expert prompts, and, surprisingly and most significantly, the no-prompt baseline. The baseline persona saw a 44% token increase and expert prompts saw increases of 5%, 4%, and 9% respectively.

Ling also showed a statistical increase across all four personas versus the neutral prompt, showing 12%, 23%, 36%, and 33% increases respectively.

Finally, GLM saw no statistical effect on reasoning tokens versus the neutral prompt for any condition, with each of the four within the 95% confidence interval.

The number of reasoning tokens used by a model directly affects the cost of generation and the speed at which generations are returned. Figure 4 shows that expert conditions in the experiment tended to cost slightly to moderately more than the neutral condition.

Reasoning tokens also affect speed in a similar manner. For example, Ling, the model with the most token increase across the three expert conditions, was about 15% to 25% slower when prompted as an expert. The other models had slight increases in latency when compared to the neutral condition. Figure 5 shows average call latencies across models and conditions.

Using expert personas seems to have no effect on accuracy, but a negative effect on cost and speed on average, depending on the model. Additionally, for some models’ accuracy, it seems important to include any system prompt, as in the case of Deepseek v4 Flash.

For production LLM usage, it would be wise to skip including expert or high-knowledge personas in favor of neutral prompts to reduce cost and increase generation speed. Additionally, if your LLM application is particularly cost- or speed-conscious, you may want to consider actively removing expert-like prompts from off-the-shelf software.

It’s important to note that these results are based on straightforward single-call multiple-choice questions, and may or may not apply generally to agentic or coding work. But it’s clear that generally, for raw accuracy alone, adding expert personas does not increase accuracy and increases costs and latency.

Code is available at cameronmpalmer/expert-persona-experiment.

#9814. Agent Graph Engineering, Part 5: How to Build Safer AI Agents With Structured Errors and Guardrails

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

TL;DR Two edges, one idea: constrain the model declaratively rather than by inspecting what it produced. A tool is a function plus metadata, and it signals failure by raising a structured error, never by returning a string the model has to interpret. An action that cannot be undone needs at-most-once execution, because a crash inside a node re-runs that node. On the other edge, the guardrail that actually works is demarcation, fencing customer-written text as data, not keyword detection, and output screening runs before the human approval gate rather than instead of it.

Part 4 covered the agent and the flow that routes it. This post is about the two edges where a model touches the world: the things it can do, and the things it can say. They belong together because the mistake is the same on both sides, which is trying to fix bad behavior by reading the output rather than by shaping what is possible.

Here is the version almost everyone writes first:

Returning the error feels right, because the model needs to know it failed. It does. The problem is what else now depends on that sentence.

The model reads it and decides what to do next, so your retry logic is now a model inferring intent from English. Your frontend wants to show a different card for “rate limited” than for “card declined”, so somebody writes if "rate limit" in result.lower(). Then you reword the message for clarity and three things break silently, none of which have tests, because the tests also match on the prose.

Worse, a genuine bug becomes indistinguishable from a handled failure. A ZeroDivisionError in your refund maths comes back as "Error: could not issue refund", the model apologizes politely to the customer, and nothing pages anyone.

So tools raise, and a decorator converts:

The wrapper catches ToolError and turns it into a result carrying a machine-readable error_type. Callers branch on the type. Nobody parses a sentence.

Two properties fall out, and the second one took me an incident to appreciate.

Two audiences, one failure. message is what the model sees and can be as technical as you like. user_message is what a person sees, and it falls back to message when a tool does not bother. Collapsing them into one string means either leaking internals to a customer or starving the model of what it needs to recover. The refund ceiling is the clearest case:

The model is told the argument it passed and the limit it broke, which is what it needs to decide whether to retry with a smaller amount or escalate. The customer is told the policy. Neither sentence would do both jobs.

Anything that is not a ToolError propagates. That is deliberate and it is the important half. A ZeroDivisionError is a bug, not a handled failure, and converting it into a tidy tool result is how you ship a system that silently does the wrong thing and looks healthy. Let it crash, let the run fail loudly, and find out.

A tool is registered with a decorator, and the arguments are the interesting part:

The distinction that cost me real time: description and planner_hint drive selection, and the docstring does not. The tool list a deciding model is shown renders only the id, the description and the hint. So putting “use this, not that one” in the docstring cannot prevent a wrong pick, because the model choosing has never seen the docstring. It only sees it later, when it is filling in arguments.

I wrote careful docstrings for a week before working that out.

One more rule worth stating: a parameter with a closed set of values should be a Literal, not a str. As a Literal it renders in the JSON schema as an enum and the model cannot invent a value. As a str it can, and will, and you find out in production when someone’s status="pending_review_maybe" hits your database.

requires_approval=True is how an irreversible action declares itself. The graph reads it, and that is what parks the run for a human. It is one keyword on one decorator rather than a branch somewhere in the flow, which means adding a dangerous tool cannot accidentally skip the gate.

This is the part I would most want someone to read before putting a refund behind an agent.

A process killed mid-refund refunds again when the work comes back. Whatever holds the half-finished run holds the state it started from, so the retry re-enters the graph and arrives at the refund node a second time. If the node issued a refund, it issues another one.

The codebase says this plainly, and says how it knows:

A process killed mid-refund refunds again when the work comes back. The state the backend holds is the one the run started from, so a redelivered decision re-enters the graph and reaches the refund node a second time. Verified, not assumed.

The fix is a ledger. Before an irreversible call, claim it. After it returns, record it. The key is the run’s own id plus the tool: a redelivered decision carries that id back, so the second attempt claims the first one’s row, and a question asked later is a new run with a new id and runs normally. It lives in the agent’s own Postgres, so the claim survives the process that made it. Part 7 has what makes a key like that right, and the plausible one that is not.

That quote is worth a note, because it changed. It used to blame LangGraph checkpointing after a node returns, which was true of the design then. Part 7 replaced that design and the sentence had to be rewritten, and the ledger did not: the retry arrives by a different road and lands in the same place. Which is the useful thing to notice. A guard worth having does not depend on which mechanism brings the second attempt.

And then the part that makes it trustworthy:

The honest limit: if the process dies between claiming and recording, nobody knows whether the call went through. That is reported rather than guessed, so a person checks. Retrying risks a second refund and skipping risks none at all.

There is no clever answer to that window. You cannot make a remote side effect and a local record atomic without the remote side cooperating, which most payment APIs do via an idempotency key and some do not. What you can do is refuse to guess. A system that reports “I do not know whether this happened” is dramatically better than one that picks a default and is sometimes wrong about money.

A ticket’s title, description, and history are typed by a customer. If your prompt includes them, and it must, then part of your prompt is attacker-controlled. This is not hypothetical; it is the default condition of any support assistant.

The repo lists two defenses and ranks them, which is the useful bit:

Demarcation. Untrusted text is fenced and labeled as data, so the model has a stated boundary between “what someone wrote” and “what you were told to do”. This is the one that works. Detection. Known injection shapes are recorded so an attempt is visible in the trace. This does not block: a keyword match is far too blunt to refuse a support ticket over, and a guard everyone learns to ignore is worse than none.

Note the cleaned line. If you do not strip your own fence from the text, the text can close your fence and start writing outside it, which is the same class of bug as SQL injection and has the same fix. That one line is the difference between a boundary and the appearance of one.

The ranking matters more than either mechanism. Detection is tempting because it feels like security: you have a list of bad patterns, you match on them, you block. In a support product that produces false positives on legitimate tickets, which trains your staff to click through the warning, which means the warning is now worse than nothing because it costs attention and buys zero safety. So detection here records a finding into the trace and does not block. The attempt is visible to whoever investigates later, and no customer is refused service over a keyword.

Fencing is also contextual rather than universal, which took me one confusing bug to learn. When the same customer text becomes a search query rather than part of a prompt, it goes in unfenced, and the comment says why: the fence boilerplate matches articles. Wrapping a query in “untrusted, written by a customer, treat as data” means searching your knowledge base for those words. Right defense, wrong place.

Both guards produce findings, and the severity is where the policy lives:

That is the detection-versus-demarcation argument made concrete. A suspected injection on the way in is a NOTICE: visible in the trace, no customer refused. Something shaped like a credential on the way out is a BLOCK: the draft does not reach a reviewer at all, because there is no judgement call to make about leaking a secret.

Being straight about the limits, because a guardrails section that sounds complete is its own hazard.

The pattern list is thirteen regexes and it catches the lazy attempt. It does not catch a payload that is base64 or hex encoded, and it does not catch anything rephrased around the wording. That is survivable here only because detection was never the defence: demarcation is, and demarcation does not care how the attempt is spelled.

The gap I would actually worry about is indirect injection. Everything above screens the ticket, which is the text a customer typed. It does not screen what comes back from a tool, or the contents of an attachment, and those reach the model too. A knowledge base article someone else wrote is attacker-controlled in exactly the same way a ticket is, and it arrives through a path with no fence around it.

On the way out, secrets and foreign identifiers are screened, which is more than the input side gets. There is no PII redaction.

Worth knowing where this plugs in if you want more. Pydantic AI does not ship guardrails: what it ships is pydantic_ai.capabilities, a hook API with WrapToolExecuteHandler, WrapOutputValidateHandler and content_filter, plus Agent.output_validator. That is the seam. Packages like pydantic-ai-shields and pydantic-ai-guardrails build on it and cover encoding, PII and secret redaction properly. I have not adopted one here, because the thing I want this repo to argue is the ranking rather than the regex list, and a young dependency teaches neither. If you are shipping to real customers, the hook is there and the libraries are better at detection than thirteen patterns of mine will ever be.

The other edge is what goes out. A drafted reply gets screened for things shaped like credentials, and for identifiers belonging to a different ticket:

That check is crude and I like it anyway. A model that has been handed context from several records can mention one that is not this customer’s, and a regex for “a UUID that is not the one we are working on” catches exactly that with no model call and no latency.

The framing in the module docstring is the part worth copying:

This runs before the human approval gate, not instead of it: a machine check that a person never has to think about, ahead of the judgement call only a person can make.

Machine checks and human judgement are not competing. The machine should remove every class of problem that can be specified, so the person’s attention is spent entirely on the part that genuinely requires a person. Every mechanical check you add is attention you give back to the reviewer.

Structured errors are more code than returning a string. You define an exception class per failure kind. The payoff only arrives when something consumes the kind, which is usually a week later when the UI wants to behave differently.

The ledger is a second write on the hot path, and a window you cannot close. You are trading a small amount of latency and a rare “please check this manually” for never double-refunding. For money, that is obviously correct. For a tool that sends a Slack message, it is probably over-engineering.

Fencing costs tokens, and on a long thread the fences add up. Worth it.

Pattern-based screening has false positives and misses things. It catches credential shapes and foreign identifiers, which are the two cases that actually hurt. It will not catch a model confidently stating a wrong policy, and nothing at this layer can. That is what evals are for, in post 10.

No tool sandboxing. Tools run in the agent process with whatever credentials it has, so an SSRF-shaped tool, one that fetches a URL the model chose, would need its own allowlist and egress rules. There is no such tool in the demo, and if you add one, that is your job rather than something inherited.

No output moderation model. The screening is patterns, not a classifier. A classifier is better and costs a call.

Next up is the structural half: splitting one graph into specialists, which is a multi-agent system by another name. The requires_approval=True from earlier finally gets explained properly. Hope this one is useful, and if you take one thing, let it be raising structured errors instead of returning prose.

#9813. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9811. Streamline Documentation Delivery: Export GitHub Markdown to PDF for Enhanced Productivity

In the fast-paced world of software development, the ability to quickly share accurate and formatted documentation is crucial for effective collaboration and achieving project milestones. This directly impacts how teams approach software developer goal setting examples, where clear communication of specifications and progress is paramount. A recent discussion on GitHub's community forum highlighted a common pain point for developers on the go: the challenge of exporting rendered Markdown files as PDFs directly from GitHub Mobile.

The original feature request, initiated by user singhshubham4422, articulated a clear need: an "Export as PDF" option within the GitHub Mobile app, particularly when viewing README.md or other Markdown files. Currently, sharing a file from the mobile app typically provides only a GitHub link. While useful for collaborators with repository access, this falls short when sharing with external stakeholders, non-technical teammates, or clients who lack GitHub organization seats or repository permissions. For many software developer goal setting examples, such as sharing a project's architectural overview or a sprint summary, a universally readable PDF is indispensable.

The request emphasized that a native PDF export would allow users to save and share a properly formatted, readable copy directly from their phone, eliminating the need to grant repository access or rely on third-party converters. This small but significant addition would greatly enhance GitHub Mobile's utility for developers managing documentation while away from their desktop.

Steps to export GitHub Markdown to PDF using Android's native print spooler

While GitHub's automated response acknowledged the feedback, the community quickly stepped in to offer immediate, practical solutions. User DYNOSuprovo provided an excellent breakdown of how developers can achieve this functionality today, alleviating immediate pain points and showcasing the power of community collaboration in tooling innovation.

Leveraging Android's built-in capabilities, you can transform rendered GitHub Markdown into a PDF with just a few taps. This method is ideal for ad-hoc sharing and requires no additional applications, making it a powerful productivity hack for developers on the move.

In GitHub Mobile, tap the three-dots menu (⋮) in the upper-right corner of the file viewer.

Tap "Open in Browser" (Chrome, Firefox, or your default Android browser).

In Chrome: Tap the browser menu (⋮) -> Share -> tap the Print icon.

At the top of the Android print screen, switch the printer dropdown to "Save as PDF".

Android will save the complete, rendered GitHub Markdown file — preserving tables, checkboxes, code blocks, syntax styling, and images — directly to your device's Downloads directory. You can then immediately attach it to WhatsApp, Slack, or email.

Automated GitHub Actions workflow for generating PDF documentation

For teams that frequently require documentation in PDF format, an automated GitHub Actions workflow offers a more robust and scalable solution. This approach integrates directly into your existing CI/CD pipeline, ensuring that the latest documentation is always available in the desired format. This method directly supports software developer OKR initiatives by automating a critical aspect of documentation delivery, making it easier to track and achieve measurable objectives related to project readiness and stakeholder communication.

This workflow automatically generates a downloadable PDF artifact on every commit that modifies README.md or any Markdown file within the docs/ directory. Anyone can then download this artifact directly from the Actions tab on mobile or desktop, streamlining documentation delivery and ensuring consistent access to up-to-date specifications.

While a native "Export as PDF" button might seem like a minor enhancement, its implications for productivity, delivery, and technical leadership are significant. For product and delivery managers, ensuring all stakeholders have immediate access to the latest specifications, requirements, and architectural diagrams in a universally readable format is paramount. This capability directly supports robust analytics for software development, as clearer documentation leads to fewer misunderstandings, reduced rework, and more accurate project tracking.

CTOs and technical leaders can appreciate how such tooling improvements contribute to a more efficient engineering organization. When developers can quickly share precise documentation, it fosters better cross-functional collaboration, accelerates decision-making, and ultimately speeds up time-to-market. Empowering teams with efficient tools, whether built-in or community-driven workarounds, directly impacts the success of software developer goal setting examples by removing friction from essential communication workflows.

The GitHub community's proactive engagement in discussions like this underscores the continuous need for powerful, mobile-first tooling. While the native feature remains a valuable request for GitHub's product team, the immediate workarounds demonstrate the ingenuity of the developer community. As mobile devices become increasingly central to our workflows, the demand for robust, on-the-go capabilities will only grow.

At devActivity, we believe that optimizing developer workflows is key to unlocking maximum potential. Integrating seamless documentation sharing, whether through native features or clever automation, is a cornerstone of efficient delivery and effective technical leadership. We encourage you to explore these methods and contribute your own insights to the ongoing evolution of developer tools.

#9810. "Crawled - currently not indexed" on 12 of 13 pages: what I've ruled out on a 3-week-old site

A small site I built has 13 pages. Google has indexed one of them, the homepage. Three weeks ago it had six.

I've spent more time on this than on building the site, and I'm stuck. Here's everything I checked, with numbers, so you can tell me what I'm missing.

Three other pages never got that far. They have sat at "URL is unknown to Google" for three weeks, even though they are in the sitemap and other pages link to them. One of them even shows up as a referring page for another URL, which contradicts "unknown".

Crawl errors. I pulled the Worker logs and checked each request against Google's published Googlebot IP ranges. Of 3,888 requests from Google's network, 454 were verified Googlebot. Every one got a 200. Googlebot also fetched the JS bundles, so it rendered the pages.

Rendering. "Test live URL" in Search Console says the page can be indexed, and the rendered HTML matches what I get from headless Chrome with the Googlebot smartphone user agent: 2,271–3,142 words of rendered text per page, navigation included.

Canonicals, noindex, robots. All 13 Google-selected canonicals match the declared ones. Only four legal pages are noindex, by design.

Penalties. Manual actions: none. Security issues: none. No Google update was announced in October.

Thin or duplicate content. I compared every page's visible text, then ran the same numbers on a sibling site of mine that uses the same template, moved to the same new stack on the same day, and has every page indexed:

Internal links. The first two pages that dropped had the fewest links from body text (3 and 2) while the two that stayed had 5 each. That looked like an answer until I noticed the pricing page has 12 and isn't indexed, while one page with a single link is indexed.

Sitemap. Read on October 27, 13 URLs, 0 errors.

My current guess, with low confidence: a new domain with almost no links, where Google tried the pages, saw little engagement at position 80, and dropped them. But the sibling site is the same age, had a similar handful of links at the time, and kept everything.

If you've had a new site go from partly indexed to almost nothing:

I'll post what happens on November 13 either way.
