#9777. StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.

Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:

These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.

To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.

We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.

We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.

When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.

We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.

Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.

As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

Here's what the data showed, and how it shaped the 9 products I launched on Nov 1.

Notion templates cluster in a three-tier ladder: $18 entry, $79 mid, $149 pro. Nobody wins with a single price â the ladder IS the pricing strategy.

Info books / playbooks sell at $20-90. Under $10 reads as "thin content" in this category.

Design assets run $36-99. Higher than most beginners guess.

The most consistent signal in the data: top products in crowded categories price UNDER the category median. Not because their content is worth less â because they're farming reviews first.

Reviews are Gumroad's discovery currency. The algorithm surfaces them, buyers filter by them. A 0-rating $29 product is invisible; a 50-rating $12 product gets discovered and can raise prices later.

Titles of bestsellers almost always promise ONE concrete outcome: a 30-day plan, a specific workflow, a named result. The "Ultimate Guide to X" pattern underperforms everywhere in the data.

In 2 of my 14 categories, the top-ranked products cost $0. You cannot build a business competing with free. Knowing which categories to avoid is arguably more valuable than knowing where to play.

#9773. WriteFreely: 49 title matches and an administrator who may be the first user

WriteFreely is a federated publishing platform with a small public footprint in this measurement. On 2026-11-04, ZoomEye returned 49 matches for title="WriteFreely" and zero for app="WriteFreely" with page 1, page size 1 and sub_type=all. A small count does not remove the need to review ownership. A publishing instance can contain unpublished drafts, API tokens and account recovery state.

WriteFreely documentation notes that in some setups the first user to log in becomes the administrator. That behavior can be appropriate for a private instance, but it is dangerous when an installation is exposed before the administrator has been claimed. The setup process must happen inside a controlled network window, with the intended administrator identity established before public discovery.

Inventory the public blog, login path, API endpoint and admin configuration. Check whether federation is enabled and whether instance registration is open. Confirm that the admin claim state is intentional and that a second administrator path cannot be created by an anonymous visitor.

WriteFreely's API documentation describes authentication for actions that create or manage content, while some read operations are public. An API token can represent a publishing account and may have a different blast radius from the server administrator. Record which API tokens exist, what they can do and when they were last used.

Do not place an API token in a public theme, client-side script or repository. Rotate it after a contributor leaves. Check that the token endpoint is protected and that logs do not contain the authorization header.

The absence of an application fingerprint means title matches should not be collapsed into a product count. For owned assets, the title is enough to find the host and compare it with inventory. For external assets, collect only public response metadata.

The 49-title population is manageable, but it is not a vulnerability list. Each result needs a reason to investigate and a boundary that stops before account enumeration or content access.

The 49 matches are a bounded discovery set. The zero application result is a warning that product-specific search will not provide full coverage. An operator can use the title set to compare external visibility with an inventory of owned domains, then verify the highest-risk installations through their own administrator console.

WriteFreely's exposure is often a combination of a public reading surface and a private publishing authority. The security decision is whether those two surfaces are deliberately separated.

#9770. Your GitHub Actions Cron Job Can Disappear Without Failing

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Every morning, a bot posts a short report to Slack: what moved volume and revenue yesterday, driver by driver. It runs on a GitHub Actions schedule and checks its own numbers before it posts. For a small team, it's a good setup. There's no server to babysit, the logs and secrets live in one place, and anyone on the team can read the run history.

It's also a scheduler with fine print, and nearly all of the fine print is about the morning the report doesn't arrive. Here's what GitHub's documentation says about scheduled workflows, what it means for a daily report, and the safeguards that make up for it.

These are all in GitHub's docs for the schedule event, roughly in order of how likely they are to bite.

Scheduled runs can be late, and some never happen. GitHub warns that scheduled runs can be delayed when Actions is under heavy load, that the start of every hour is one of those times, and that under enough load "some queued jobs may be dropped." A dropped run doesn't fail. It just doesn't happen.

Schedules run in UTC unless you say otherwise. Schedules now accept a timezone with an IANA name like America/New_York. Without it, a 7 AM report drifts to 6 AM or 8 AM local twice a year when daylight saving time changes. With it, a time that doesn't exist on the spring-forward day moves to the next valid time.

Schedules only run from the default branch, on its latest commit. Editing a workflow on a feature branch won't tell you whether its schedule works.

In public repositories, schedules switch off after 60 days with no repository activity. A report that just works for two months and then stops is the most frustrating version of all of this.

The shortest interval is five minutes. Irrelevant for a daily report, worth knowing before you build a poller on it.

Most of those lines answer the fine print. The cron is 17 7, not 0 7, because the top of the hour is the busiest time, and a report at 7:17 that arrives beats one at 7:00 that doesn't. workflow_dispatch adds a "Run workflow" button for the mornings the schedule doesn't fire. concurrency stops a manual run and a late scheduled run from overlapping. And the QA rules run as tests before the report does, so a change to the rules can't quietly switch them off.

A daily report should never post a number it can't defend. Before anything goes to the channel, run checks like these:

When a check fails, the report goes to its owner instead of the channel:

Each rule has its own unit test. A held report is a good outcome. It means the bot caught something before a room full of people did.

Retries and manual reruns are good for reliability and bad for a Slack channel. Before posting, check whether today's report is already there:

The marker is the report's own title. A rerun after a successful post does nothing, and a rerun after a held report posts normally once the data is fixed.

None of those checks help when the run never starts. A dropped schedule doesn't fail, so nothing alerts. The answer is a second workflow that runs later and asks one question: did today's report succeed?

It isn't perfect. The watchdog runs on the same scheduler with the same fine print, so it's a second chance, not a guarantee. For a report that really matters, have the bot ping an external heartbeat monitor when it succeeds, and let that service complain when the ping doesn't come. The principle is the same either way: alert on the absence of success, not the presence of failure.

When a report has to arrive at a specific minute, or runs often enough that a few dropped runs a month would matter, use a scheduler that makes promises: a cloud scheduler, Airflow, or a plain cron server you monitor. For one report a day that can arrive at 7:17 or 7:24 without anyone noticing, GitHub Actions is hard to beat. Just read the fine print, and build for the morning it doesn't show up.

#9767. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.

#9766. Scrambled Eggs Won't Be Same When You Grab A Canned Staple With Extra Protein

For a lot of people, scrambled eggs are a go-to when it comes time for a hot, savory breakfast. And why not? They're quick and easy to make, and they've long been considered the gold standard for protein, coming in at roughly 6 to 7 grams apiece.

All that said, though, on their own, scrambled eggs are more of a side, but if you want to make them main meal-worthy, adding one staple ingredient will not only bring more flavor into the mix, but a great deal of extra protein, too. Canned tuna is the game-changer here — it infuses your eggs with a savory umami flavor reminiscent of the sea, as well as a satisfyingly meaty texture.

You could partially scramble your eggs, then add the tuna and continue to cook until the eggs are set, or even mix the tuna and raw, cracked eggs in a bowl and pour both into the pan together. But we highly recommend working in steps, first draining the liquid from the can (don't rinse the fish!) and crisping up the tuna in a hot skillet with some oil, then adding the eggs and cooking until they're set. This gives the tuna a delightful texture boost, and it makes for a much more interesting bite with the contrasting crispy bits of the fish and the softness of the eggs.

Tuna and scrambled eggs are endlessly modifiable, which is great if you take comfort in making the same dishes on repeat, but need a little flavor variation. You might try first switching up the tuna you're using; StarKist's Flavor Fresh Pouch line, for example, has a wide selection of flavors, everything from Honey BBQ to Jalapeño to Thai Chili. Even better, you don't have to drain anything — you can just dump the tuna straight from the pouch into the skillet.

If you're looking to build a little flavor in the oil before you add the tuna, though, you might chop or mince some fresh onion or garlic, respectively. Red onion in particular is an excellent aromatic to use because it imbues the whole dish with a kiss of sweetness that contrasts deliciously with the savory elements. Or you might really lean into the fish factor with a splash of fish sauce and a liquid sweetener, like honey or maple syrup, both to develop deep, savory notes and to allow the sugars to promote super-flavorful caramelization of the tuna.

And then there are toppings. A sprinkle of green onion would add an appealing brightness and bite to this dish, while those looking for outright spice might finish off the tuna and scrambled eggs with a drizzle of hot sauce or sriracha. Or you could shovel the tuna-and-egg combination onto sturdy pieces of toast and top with avocado and plenty of everything bagel seasoning.

#9763. Pour Cream Over Diced Potatoes For A Southern-Style Side (Hint: It's Not Gratin)

Cream and potatoes go together better than peanut butter and jelly, and with only a few extra fixings, you can get a seriously Southern-style side dish with very little effort. By just combining potatoes, seasoning, and cream, you get Creole potatoes, a rustic, flavorful recipe with tons of room for experimentation. Enter: Creole cream potatoes.

When it comes to Creole cooking, you'll often find some sort of vegetable gratin on the menu. However, whereas a standard gratin relies on a roux to thicken a cream sauce, this recipe keeps the sauce a bit thinner. Using Creole spice mix instead of Cajun is also quite important, as the higher ratio of herbs pairs perfectly with a bit of cheese, dairy fat, and tubers. While you still want a bit of spice, the parsley, oregano, thyme, and other woody herbs diffuse their flavorful oils into the sauce to then be absorbed by the potatoes.

Since you won't be able to taste this dish as you go, you may want to use a different kind of butter than your usual salted variety. Unsalted ones give you maximum control and, while potatoes do absorb sodium quite well, this is important so that you don't spend an hour baking a dish you later find unpalatable. Most of the baking time for this recipe calls for it to be covered, but don't forget a final few minutes uncovered or even under the broiler to crisp up a last layer of cheese and roast any exposed parts of the potatoes. A little crunch in a swimming rich sauce of cream? Yes, please.

When you're working with such a simple dish, there's always room to add new ingredients or try out new preparation methods. Whether you're picking out different potatoes for a new texture, finding the right balance of fat, or even tossing in some protein, it's hard to go wrong with something this straightforward.

If you like your sauce to be a bit thicker, something that clings to the vegetables, try using russet potatoes. Affordable and available most anywhere, these come loaded with starch but have very little moisture, making them perfect for baking with dairy. This same thing makes them the best variety of spud for scalloped potatoes as they're great at absorbing fat and keeping that flavor on your fork rather than pooling at the bottom of the dish. If you want to keep your sauce thin, aim for a waxier potato, like fingerlings, new potatoes, or any red variety.

Speaking of fat, the one downside of any cream- and butter-based recipe is that it's easy to make it overly greasy. Full-fat cream is vital to getting the right mouthfeel and flavor for the sauce, but you can always use a lower-fat butter or leaner protein as your main. Leaving fat out of other ingredients can also be an opportunity for adding it back through other means. Few things are more Creole than classic potatoes and sausage, but if you want to have less oil, there's no protein more lean and Louisiana than shrimp.

#9759. James Bond Ate This Vintage Breakfast You Rarely See On Menus Anymore

Whether it's the Rolex watches or a seemingly endless supply of Aston Martins, few encapsulate luxury quite like James Bond. The iconic spy from Ian Fleming's novels has long been a cultural icon, and his taste for the finer things extends well beyond material possessions. When it comes to dining, everyone knows his "shaken, not stirred" martini order, along with his fondness for Bollinger Champagne, scrambled eggs, and Beluga caviar. But only eagle-eyed fans who have read Fleming's 1958 novel "Dr No" may recall 007 tucking into grilled kidneys, an old-school delicacy that's seriously underrated by modern diners.

In the novel, Bond is held captive by the titular villain, but his captors don't exactly skimp on the prison food. His morning meal consisted of scrambled eggs on toast, four rashers of bacon, an English pork sausage, and a grilled kidney, alongside rolls, preserves, pineapple juice, and coffee with cream. It's a surprisingly lavish spread for a prisoner, although the kidney may raise a few eyebrows among younger readers. Back in the day, however, offal was a favorite amongst boomers, and kidneys were a welcome addition to a hearty breakfast.

Kidneys were a part of a long tradition of morning meals, particularly among the well-to-do during the Victorian and Edwardian eras, so it was almost inevitable that they'd later feature in a Bond novel. Back in the early 20th century, you could expect to find this dish served at all manner of haughty establishments, like the Fairmont San Francisco, and they're still served for breakfast at London's ultra-fancy Dorchester Hotel. Fleming leaves how they're prepared to the imagination, but one common recipe involves halving the kidneys lengthways, removing the tough inner core, and grilling both sides for no more than three minutes, brushing them with butter throughout.

Beyond looking as suave as Bond, there are plenty of reasons to give kidneys a spot on your shopping list. Aside from being relatively inexpensive, they're nutritional powerhouses, packed with protein and essential nutrients. It's also worth considering from a sustainability standpoint. Organ meats make up a substantial portion of a livestock carcass, yet they're often overlooked in favor of more familiar cuts. In fact, a 2019 study for Environmental Science & Technology examining Germany's meat industry found that increasing offal consumption by 50% could reduce the sector's greenhouse gas emissions by up to 14%, partly because adopting a nose-to-tail philosophy means fewer animals would be needed to meet demand.

One of the biggest hurdles to cooking kidneys is simply knowing where to start. They aren't your everyday chicken breast or steak, so preparing them for the first time can feel daunting. But here's the secret: They're not nearly as tricky as you might think. Pan-frying is a classic method, particularly for making deviled kidneys. Slice the kidneys in half and cut out the tough white core. Fry them in butter until browned, then add a punchy mixture of your favorite jelly, mustard, Worcestershire sauce, and a pinch of cayenne pepper. Let everything bubble together briefly, thicken the sauce with cream, and then spoon it all over buttered toast for a super traditional British breakfast.

Sometimes half the battle is getting past the idea of what you're eating. To counter this, you can even sneak kidneys into everyday meals without making them the star of the show. Ask your butcher to mince them, then mix a small amount into ground lamb or beef for a rich, savory ragù, shepherd's pie, or even homemade burger patties. If you're feeling really adventurous, skip the mince and combine the kidneys with chopped livers and heart.

#9756. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9755. The Companies Allegedly Behind 15 Trader Joe's Items

Trader Joe's is full of unique and delicious products sold under the brand's private label, but having the store's name on the package doesn't mean that's who is making those products. Like other private label retailers like Aldi and Costco, Trader Joe's keeps the identity of its vendors under wraps to help keep costs lower for consumers. This probably means very little to the average Trader Joe's customer until beloved Trader Joe's products are discontinued and the search for a suitable replacement begins.

Importantly, just because a brand is confirmed or believed to be behind a Trader Joe's product doesn't mean that the Trader Joe's item is identical to the brand's usual offering. Small recipe or ingredient changes to adhere to Trader Joe's product standards and vendor requirements aren't uncommon.

Still, knowing the vendor can help you find a close match. While the legal agreements that keep Trader Joe's brands a secret usually make it nearly impossible to confirm the companies behind the store's products, several brands have been outed over the years. This is thanks to a combination of discerning customers, loose lipped employees, and a food safety policy that errs on the side of caution, resulting in an abundance of Trader Joe's recalls.

When it comes to foods like nuts, it's nearly impossible to tell one brand from another simply by looking at them, especially if the nuts in question don't have any special seasonings or flavors. That's certainly the case for pistachios roasted in their shells, which look virtually identical across brands, but a 2016 Salmonella-related recall helped unmask the major brand behind Trader Joe's pistachios as Wonderful Pistachios.

Three versions of Trader Joe's dry roasted, in shell pistachios were included in the recall: salted, unsalted, and 50% less salt. While the shelled version of Trader Joe's pistachios (unroasted, unsalted pistachio nutmeats) were not included in the recall and therefore can't definitively be linked to Wonderful, it is notable that the packaging for the shelled version is nearly identical to the dry roasted, in shell version, and Trader Joe's notes that both versions originate in California. Take that for what it's worth.

Salad kits and prepared salads are a convenient way to add extra veggies to your meal, and Trader Joe's has some delicious options. The brand behind those salads is one you've almost certainly heard. In August 2026, a large recall for fresh jalapeños contaminated with Salmonella had ripple effects across the food industry because of the number of brands that used the peppers in its products. Among those was Taylor Farms, which issued a recall on a number of different products, including Trader Joe's fiesta style salad with shrimp sold in Texas.

Around the same time, during a large scale outbreak of Cyclospora related illnesses also linked to Taylor Farms, an alleged Trader Joe's employee revealed on Reddit that the store sources most of its salad kits from Taylor Farms. At the time, the source of those illnesses had not yet been narrowed down to iceberg lettuce, and the seemingly well meaning employee posted the revelation as a public service announcement. The outbreak was declared over by the Centers for Disease Control on September 11, 2026.

Many Trader Joe's prepared foods and meals are perfect for a picnic, and you might be surprised how many of them are made by the same company. Bakkavor Foods USA has been behind many Trader Joe's products for at least a decade and was one of the largest producers of fresh and prepared foods in both the United States and the UK before being acquired by Greencore in 2025.

In 2016, Bakkavor issued a voluntary recall of both Trader Joe's Mediterranean Hummus and White Bean & Basil Hummus due to possible contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. But hummus isn't the only food that Bakkavor produces for Trader Joe's. Three years later in 2019, another voluntary recall was issued, again for possible listeria contamination, but this time in Trader Joe's Egg Salad and Old Fashioned Potato Salad. Then, in 2023, the company issued a recall for Trader Joe's Genova Pesto because it was incorrectly packaged and contained undeclared allergens in the form of milk and walnuts, both of which can cause serious allergic reactions.

After being acquired by Greencore, Bakkavor issued another recall in 2026 for Trader Joe's Focaccia Bread with Roasted Tomato & Parmesan. Metal fragments were discovered in the bread, which the company later said came from its roasted tomato supplier.

While the sugar content and some of the health claims made by Naked Juice have come under fire over the years, there's no denying that the brand makes delicious juice and smoothies. To hear some customers tell it, those same juices can be found at Trader Joe's.

Based on labels alone, those customers may be onto something. The ingredients in Trader Joe's Very Green 100% juice smoothie are a very close match to Naked's Green Machine and Trader Joe's Mango 100% juice smoothie is virtually a carbon copy of Naked's Mighty Mango Machine.

While that may be as close as we can get to confirmation today, Naked Juice and Trader Joe's go back more than two decades. In 2000, when possible Salmonella contamination resulted in a fresh juice recall in California, both Naked Juice and Trader Joe's juice were included as both were sourced from California Day-Fresh Foods at the time.

Naked Juice isn't the only brand behind the juice at Trader Joe's, at least as of 2024. Back then, a recall of under-processed organic carrot juice that carried a risk of causing botulism revealed that Trader Joe's organic carrot juice was made by Barsotti. It really wasn't that much of a surprise given that the Barsotti bottle was virtually identical to the Trader Joe's bottle, from the shape all the way down (or up) to the green cap.

Still, it was good for the carrot juice lovers to get confirmation, especially because Trader Joe's does not currently sell the organic carrot juice, and many customers miss it. Based on social media posts, it seemed to disappear from Trader Joe's shelves right around the time of the recall and never reappeared.

Trader Joe's does list an organic carrot turmeric juice blend on its website, but Barsotti does not sell a similar juice blend. Still, it's possible the carrot juice in the current juice blend originates with Barsotti and is a special recipe exclusive for Trader Joe's, but at this point, that's merely speculation.

While it is just one of many Trader Joe's myths that've been debunked that the grocery store is a spot for health food, the company does have pretty stringent standards for its products, and organic foods are easy to find. Combining both organic ingredients and a popular comfort food, the organic shells and white cheddar macaroni and cheese is long believed to be the same as Annie's organic Shells & White Cheddar macaroni and cheese.

The Trader Joe's version of the creamy comfort dish has ingredients that match Annie's almost exactly. If the ingredient similarities are not evidence enough, a packaging mistake in 2026 sealed the deal. Several customers posted photos online after allegedly opening their Trader Joe's Organic Shells and White Cheddar macaroni and cheese, only to find Annie's branded white cheddar powdered cheese packets inside. Whoops. That all but confirms it for sure.

Trader Joe's customers have expressed a lot of thoughts online about the store's meat and poultry selection. Some prefer it over what they find elsewhere, while others suggest it is expensive and subpar. But, like the other private label products at Trader Joe's, it may be the same meat and poultry you've bought elsewhere under a different name.

Customers who believed the fan favorite Trader Joe's Sweet Apple Chicken Sausage was a convincing dupe for Al Fresco's version were vindicated in 2015 when a recall of Kayem chicken sausages affected both brands. At the time, both Trader Joe's Sweet Apple Chicken Sausage and Al Fresco Apple Maple Chicken Breakfast Sausage were recalled due to the possibility of contamination with small pieces of plastic.

Whether Kayem still supplies the sausages is unclear, though the Trader Joe's website suggests the sausages are unchanged since they were introduced in 2004. The October 2026 recall of over 1.5 million pounds of ready-to-eat Kayem products due to improper storage temperature does not include any Trader Joe's branded products as of this writing.

Falling in love with a seasonal tea at Trader Joe's, only to have it discontinued is a terrible feeling. Many customers have found what they believe is a workaround. Several social media threads suggest Celestial Seasonings produces Trader Joe's tea, and that you can often order even the seasonal varieties year-round.

One of the most convincing arguments is a Reddit thread that focuses on Trader Joe's Candy Cane green tea. Not only are the ingredients identical to Celestial Seasonings Candy Cane Lane green tea, the boxes bear a striking resemblance with green clad polar bears on the front and the same box shape and design. Customers also suggest that Trader Joe's discontinued Red Refresh herbal tea is almost identical to Red Zinger by Celestial Seasonings in taste, description, and packaging.

One commenter alleges that they personally saw Trader Joe's mango tea boxes when they went on the Celestial Seasonings factory tour and recounts being told by the tour guide that Celestial Seasonings makes other teas for the retailer. What we know for sure is that Celestial Seasonings publicly partnered with Trader Joe's for two exclusive tea blends in 2013 (Harvest Blend and Chai). While the company's website previously noted this as a milestone event on its history page (via Internet Archive), the information has since been removed.

Comparing Trader Joe's thin and crunchy pretzel slims with Snack Factory's original pretzel crisps, there are certainly some compelling similarities among the ingredients. Trader Joe's pretzel slims contain unbleached enriched flour, inverted sugar syrup, salt, malted barley, sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), and sodium hydroxide. Snack Factory's pretzel crisps contain enriched flour, cane sugar, salt, tapioca malt syrup, canola oil, and [baking] soda. The two varieties also share a 1-ounce serving size with matching calorie content. Thankfully, Snack Factory's dark chocolate variety is easier to find than Trader Joe's.

There's nothing like a bowl of warm soup in the fall and winter months, and few soups are as resoundingly praised as Trader Joe's organic tomato and roasted red pepper soup. Customers rave about eating the soup with grilled cheese sandwiches, macaroni and cheese balls, or even with a bit of rice mixed in to bulk it up as a standalone meal. If that has you craving a bowl for yourself but your Trader Joe's doesn't have any in stock, just pick up a carton of Pacific Food's roasted red pepper and tomato soup. A 2017 recall due to under-processing revealed they are both made by Pacific.

Although other varieties of Trader Joe's soups have not been recalled, and we therefore do not have a confirmation as to their manufacturer, the same style box that is used for the organic tomato and roasted red pepper soup (and Pacific soups) is also used for the store's organic chicken and vegetable broths, including regular and low sodium.

For folks with peanut allergies, Trader Joe's Dark Chocolate Almond Butter Cups can be a great alternative to the more common peanut butter cups. Unfortunately, a 2021 recall revealed that some of the almond butter cups might have inadvertently contained peanut protein. While the package label indicated traces of peanuts were possible, allergic reactions prompted the recall anyway. The recall also revealed the candy was produced by Bazzini.

Even if you don't know the name, you likely know the products. Bazzini started out in 1886, making it the oldest nut and confection company in the United States, and also the brand of peanuts sold at Yankee Stadium. Its chocolate confections are sold under the name Barton's and include not only dark chocolate almond butter cups, but also milk chocolate peanut butter cups and dark chocolate peanut butter cups. Both peanut butter cup varieties are also available at Trader Joe's and may also be produced by Bazzini.

Trader Joe's selection of snack foods is arguably only matched by its selection of frozen foods and meals, especially when it comes to international cuisine. It might not be too surprising to learn that the manufacturer behind at least some of these international frozen foods is Ajinomoto Foods, which purports to be the brand leader in the sector.

While we can't definitively say all the different products Ajinomoto provides to Trader Joe's, a large recall in early 2026 included Trader Joe's chicken fried rice. The recall was initially issued due to the possibility of glass fragments in several products across many different labels. Trader Joe's expanded on Ajinomoto's initial recall and included its vegetable fried rice, Japanese fried rice, and chicken Shu Mai to be on the safe side, confirming that all are Ajinomoto products. All of those are pretty popular TJ's products, too.

For those of us who love yogurt, Trader Joe's has plenty to choose from, and it's one of the few products whose origin is somewhat easy to pinpoint, even without a specific recall. In 2017, a writer for Fortune revealed that Stonyfield supplies Trader Joe's with a good deal of its yogurt, especially on the East Coast. Around the same time, a Trader Joe's employee confirmed Stonyfield was one of the store's partners during a Reddit Ask Me Anything session.

Even though Stonyfield had one of the worst yogurt recalls in history, that was also all the way back in 2017 and applied only to plant-based yogurt, none of which was recalled from Trader Joe's. But tracking the manufacturer of Trader Joe's yogurt is a lot easier than some other products due to the ease with which consumers can track dairy manufacturing in the United States using the website Where Is My Milk From.

Dairy plant codes used by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) are stamped on all containers and can be traced to specific manufacturers. For example, Trader Joe's yogurt with dairy codes that begin with 33-14 originate at the Stonyfield plant in Londonderry, New Hampshire.

The holiday season is one of the best times of the year for foodies because all sorts of seasonal gourmet condiments and snacks start to hit the shelves at Trader Joe's. Among these are jams, jellies, spreads, and bar mixes, all of which can be perfect additions to holiday celebrations.

The problem is that once they're gone, they're gone. That is, unless you are a discerning customer who is able to figure out that Trader Joe's Step Up to the Snack Bar mix, discontinued garlic and onion jam, and pepper jelly are all dead ringers for the same products at Stonewall Kitchen. In particular, Trader Joe's and Stonewall Kitchen's bar mixes both contain honey roasted peanuts, honey mustard pretzels, cheddar crackers, sesame sticks, and chili lemon sticks.

Unfortunately, neither the garlic and onion jam nor the pepper jelly are currently available at Trader Joe's, but they've been known to make a comeback seasonally. If you simply can't wait, Stonewall Kitchen sells them year-round.

#9751. Not Milk: Burgers Are 10x Juicier When You Add This Ingredient

Chefs employ many strategies to moisten burger patties. Some add a dash of mayo for extra fat and flavor, while others swear by heavy cream for juicy patties. Still, there are always more mouth-watering options to explore — like buttermilk, for example. The tangy fermented dairy is often designated for giving pancakes some fluff, but lends advantages when worked into minced meat, too.

The lactic acid in buttermilk functions as an effective meat tenderizer, making a burger that's a touch juicier. The dairy's tartness is perceptible in the taste without overwhelming the palate. You don't need much to revamp a burger recipe; half a cup per a pound of beef is enough to translate buttermilk's unique effects. Simply mix and form the patties like during a traditional burger recipe, folding in supplementary ingredients like onions and breadcrumbs if desired.

Similar results in texture and flavor are also possible with buttermilk powder. The dehydrated version of the dairy is easier to work with, and still contains the signature fat and tanginess, just without the extra water. It effectively creates a crust around meats, making it widely used in Southern dry rubs. Dust a third of a cup onto a pound of meat, and you'll get a juicy burger, while helping seasonings stick. Who knew buttermilk could prove so valuable on burger night?

While the effects are primarily textural, buttermilk impacts the burger's flavor, too. The inclusion adds a lightly acidic and milky taste, setting up for complementary ingredients. You can further lean into the patty's tender flavor by adding breadcrumbs, which yield an extra-tender, meatball-like dish. Consider using a flavored crumb — say Italian-herb — and work onions and pickles into the patty, too. Topped with ingredients like fresh basil and sliced tomatoes, you'll get an extra-juicy burger that's enjoyable even when well-done.

Alternatively, you can steer the tanginess into a more spiced direction. Buttermilk is widely used in Indian cooking to absorb aromatics and the same kind of application works in a burger. Mix in store-bought curry powder or make your own blend using aromatics like cumin, coriander, and ginger. To round out the dish, top with mango chutney or a fragrant chile paste.

Finally, if you'd like to keep your burger rendition on the classic side, consider garnishing with a homemade ranch. The iconic sauce employs buttermilk, too, making a burger rendition flavored with the dairy both inside and out. Optionally paired with a couple of bacon strips, it's a flavorful riff on the dish that's bound to stay moist.

#9749. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.
